name: Why we need Advanced Practice Nurses and Midwives

content.title: Why we need Advanced Practice Nurses and Midwives
content.summary: After approval of two Master's programmes by Kenya's Commission for University Education, SONAM collaborated with the Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) on a fellowship programme for four of its faculty. Here is an intervew with two faculty

media.caption: From left: Dr Rachel Wangari, Dr Bev Jervis (Midwifery lecturer at the Liverpool John Moores University, UK), Dr Grace Nakate and Dr Eunice Siaity-Pallangyo after attending the 5th Commonwealth nurses and midwives conference in London
media.alt: Why we need Advanced Practice Nurses and Midwives

content.text: AKU's School of Nursing and Midwifery (SONAM) not only offers academic training for practising nurses and midwives but also provides its faculty opportunities for career development. Following approval of two Master's programmes by Kenya's Commission for University Education, SONAM collaborated with the Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) on a fellowship programme for four of its faculty. The fellowship began on February 24, 2020, and was to last six weeks but was cut short by the COVID-19 pandemic. The four faculty were Dr Eunice Siaity-Pallangyo, Academic Head, SONAM Tanzania; Dr Rachel Kimani, faculty, SONAM Kenya; Dr Grace Nakate, faculty SONAM Uganda; and Ms Lucy Kisaka, faculty, SONAM  Tanzania.
We spoke to Dr Rachel Kimani and Dr Grace Nakate on their experience at LJMU as well as their thoughts on the importance of better-qualified nurses and midwives.
Why did you go to LJMU?

We went to benchmark and develop our capacity on how to go about the Advanced Practice Nursing and Midwifery (APN and APM) programmes as we prepare to offer them at SONAM as well. It was important as LJMU is one of the best universities in healthcare research and education in the UK.
What activities were you involved in during the fellowship?

We interacted with Advanced Practice programme teams, benchmarked our curriculum with LJMU's and learned from each other, attended various Master-level lectures to find out how sessions are conducted, attended continuous professional development sessions where we learned how to use social media to teach large classes and to top it all off, we attended the 5
Commonwealth Nurses and Midwives Conference in London.
Who are Advanced Practice Nurses and Midwives?

Being an Advanced Practice Nurse, I realized that there is a misconception that we are 'mini-doctors' or doctor's assistants or nurse managers. Not exactly. SONAM's APN and APM programmes will provide East African healthcare systems with graduate-level nurses and midwives who will work at advanced capacity because of the knowledge and skills they will have to administer effective care and improve outcomes for our patients.

Nurses comprise over 70 % of Kenya's healthcare workforce and are usually at the frontline of healthcare systems, as seen during the COVID-19 crisis. Due to a lack of qualified medical practitioners in Kenya, especially in rural settings, nurses have been practising at advanced levels regardless of their defined roles, formal graduate education or license. This is why SONAM deemed it necessary to pioneer the APN and APM programmes: to create nurses and midwives with an expert knowledge base and complex decision-making abilities.
Why is it important for nurses and midwives to advance their education?

Nurses and midwives who work independently at lower-level health facilities in East Africa usually have the lowest educational qualifications. The Master's trained nurses and midwives are either in education or leadership, yet their services are highly required at all levels of practice. Many of the facilities in the community and rural areas are managed by medical assistants who do not know enough about nursing practice and evidence-based practice. Therefore, it is crucial to train Advanced Practice nurses and midwives who will promote evidence-based practice and leadership at all levels of care. Since there are more nurses and midwives than doctors in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania, it is important to equip them with the necessary knowledge and skills to handle healthcare challenges and make essential decisions from rural settings to urban ones.
Even as we benchmark with LJMU, we have contextualized it to our needs in East Africa. We will continue to build and improve the programmes as we move forward.
